The words

Who has believ'd thy word,
Or thy salvation known?
Reveal thine arm, almighty Lord,
And glorify thy Son.

The Jews esteem'd him here
Too mean for their belief:
Sorrows his chief acquaintance were,
And his companion, grief.

They turn'd their eyes away,
And treated him with scorn;
But 'twas their grief upon him lay,
Their sorrows he has borne.

'Twas for the stubborn Jews,
And Gentiles then unknown,
The God of justice pleas'd to bruise
His best beloved Son.

"But I'll prolong his days,
"And make his kingdom stand,
"My pleasure, (saith the God of grace)
"Shall prosper in his hand.

"His joyful soul shall see
"The purchase of his pain,
"And by his knowledge justify
"The guilty sons of men.

"Ten thousand captive slaves,
"Releas'd from death and sin,
"Shall quit their prisons and their graves;
"And own his power divine.

"Heaven shall advance my Son
"To joys that earth deny'd;
"Who saw the follies men had done,
"And bore their sins, and dy'd."

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Bb and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on l, (G), on the word “Who”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts wrote these words for his Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), Book I, collected from the Scriptures, hymn 141, headed “The humiliation and exaltation of Christ, Isa. 53. 1-5 10 11 12”.

Watts' hymns were printed without tunes and sung to any tune of their metre, Short Metre (6.6.8.6). This page sets the words to ST. BRIDE; any other Short Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Music (1762): Samuel Howard (died undefined)

Tune ST. BRIDE by Samuel Howard (died undefined); words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748).

Sung to the same tune: Behold What Wondrous Grace, Exalt the Lord Our God, Here, in This Place of Prayer, Let God the Maker's Name, Let Sinners Take Their Course, Lord What a Feeble Piece, My Saviour and My King, My Soul, Repeat His Praise, Not with Our Mortal Eyes, Now Let Our Voices Join, O Blessed Souls Are They, O Lord, Our Heavenly King, Raise Your Triumphant Songs, Teach Me, My God and King, The Man Is Ever Blest, We Love This Outward World, When Man Grows Bold in Sin, Where Shall the Man Be Found, Ye Servants of the Lord.

Questions about Who Has Believ'd Thy Word

What is the doh of Who Has Believ'd Thy Word?

In this version, in G minor, doh is Bb. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Who Has Believ'd Thy Word start on?

It starts on l, (G in G minor), a pickup on the word “Who” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to l,.

Is Who Has Believ'd Thy Word in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Samuel Howard died in undefined; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1762. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
